Some low cost finance available but not yet universally acessible

National residential PV subsidies (FiT) were fully phased out in 2021–2022. Green credit lines and fiscal discount interest support PV-related investment, and the "Whole County PV" model mobilises developer/lease financing, but there is no universal national low-interest consumer loan or rebate programme for household BTM technology.

Confirms FiT phase-out and availability of fiscal discount interest/green finance for PV industry projects; no evidence of a universal retail consumer low-cost finance scheme.

Behind-the-meter technology affordable and accessible to all earners inc. through zero capital cost models

Hardware costs are the lowest globally thanks to domestic manufacturing. Rural and lower-income households can access systems at zero capital cost through roof-leasing/developer models under the Whole County PV programme. However, red-zone connection suspensions in 11 provinces (2024) block access regardless of income.

IEA reports 2024 connection restrictions in 11 provinces where DPV injection exceeded hosting capacity — a geographic, not income-based, restriction. Zero-capital developer/leasing models widely documented.

Cost of finance for behind-the-meter technology available at or below 5%

Developer-side and green-loan finance is available at rates at or below ~5% (LPR-linked green credit plus fiscal interest discounts for PV projects), enabling the massive distributed build-out (118 GW distributed in 2024). Consumer-rate finance for households is scarcer, but scale finance demonstrably exists.

Fiscal discount interest policy explicitly reduces financing costs for PV-related industry; 2024 distributed additions of ~118 GW indicate scalable finance at developer level.

No universal best practices or standards in place

No single national standard exists for consumer-facing benefit calculation/communication. The Whole County model standardised contracts and access, but benefit communication varies by province and developer; post-2025 market pricing (noon off-peak windows) has made legacy benefit projections misleading for new customers.

The NSR describes standardised filing and technical standards but no nationally mandated methodology for communicating investment returns; Document 136 reforms materially changed PV export value, outdating older consumer guidance. Score refined downward from my Stage 2 summary based on this review.

Network operators face some barriers to operating / incentivising / contracting with or owning behind-the-meter technology

Grid companies are legally barred from owning competitive generation assets following the 2015 power sector reform, but they can procure services from and contract with aggregated BTM resources. The "one county, one developer" model further concentrates ownership outside networks/operators.

2015 reform separated grid operation from generation ownership; grid companies act as monopoly network operators and buyers, not asset owners. Some provincial pilots allow grid-affiliated aggregation, hence "some barriers".

Time of use pricing for electricity import available to some customers

Mandatory TOU pricing applies to essentially all C&I customers (universally in the market since 2022), and market-based TOU retail pricing is accelerating. Residential customers in many provinces have TOU options, but universal residential spot-linked pricing is not yet complete.

RMI identifies strengthening wholesale-retail price pass-through and accelerating retail-side market-based TOU pricing as ongoing 2026 trends; Document No. 165622 (effective March 2026) phases out regulated TOU for market participants, while grid-delegated buyers retain regulated TOU — hence "almost all" rather than all.

Export pricing available but restricted to only one form of behind-the-meter technology or not available to all customers

Since the Feb 2025 NDRC/NEA reform (Document 136), exported power from distributed solar is settled at market-based or mechanism prices with TOU differentiation, and midday off-peak pricing is cutting export values. Many existing household systems retain legacy arrangements, and participation rules vary by province.

NSR documents the Feb 9, 2025 Notice on market-based reform of new energy feed-in tariffs; over 50% of new energy generation now integrated through market mechanisms. Storage-friendly pricing (PV + Storage configurations) is growing. Availability to all customers, including household solar and storage exporters, is not yet uniform.

Bills broken down to show all of the following: wholesale/energy costs / network costs / system operation and taxes (where these are applicable)

National policy requires itemised bills showing energy/purchase costs, transmission & distribution tariffs, system operation fees, government funds & surcharges, and taxes. Depth of breakdown is strongest for market participants; some residential bills remain simplified.

T&D tariff reform established cost-plus reasonable-profit itemised network charges; electricity bills across provinces list energy, network, system operation, fund and tax components.

Data is available in an electronic fomat online

Smart meter penetration is near-universal, with data available electronically (via utility apps/portals) at 15-minute resolution in spot-market pilot provinces and half-hourly or better for settled market customers.

Settlement is shifting to monthly pricing or near-real-time settlement intervals of 15 minutes in pilots, implying sub-half-hourly metering infrastructure at scale.

Behind-the-meter technology have size barriers 50% or more of the wholesale and ancillary markets which are open to behind-the-meter technology

Yes. Minimum aggregation/capacity thresholds commonly apply for ancillary market entry (multi-MW scale), and new distributed PV rules restrict large C&I projects above 6 MW to full self-consumption with no grid sales, while small distributed systems are often exempted or channelled through aggregation.

Documents that full grid access was cancelled for C&I projects, with standard projects up to 6 MW able to partially export and projects above 6 MW required to fully self-consume. Individual small BTM assets generally cannot enter wholesale/ancillary markets directly.

All ancillary and wholesale markets pricing is fully transparent

Spot and ancillary market outcomes are published by provincial trading centres (typically next-day for spot prices), and ancillary service compensation rules are public documents. Pricing is transparent but not universally available in real time.

Details evolution from planned compensation to market-oriented ancillary mechanisms with published rules; provincial trading centres publish spot clearing results. Real-time publication for all products is not yet universal.

VPPs have access to no more than 50% of wholesale or ancillary markets which are open to behind-the-meter technology

The 2024 Basic Rules for Power Market Operation give virtual power plants, energy storage, load aggregators and V2G operators legal market-participant status, with active provincial VPP pilots (Guangdong, Zhejiang, Shenzhen). Actual access remains provincial-pilot dependent and aggregated rather than individual; rural distributed PV is excluded in some provincial markets (e.g. western Inner Mongolia, Gansu exceptions).

Confirms storage and VPPs have made progress in spot-market participation and that western Inner Mongolia and Gansu exclude distributed PV from certain market participation. VPP market still in early scale-up.

Compensation available to all behind-the-meter technology that meet required technical standards but only under trials

Locational signals exist via spot pricing and hosting-capacity zoning, and pilots exist for distributed resources deferring network reinforcement, but routine, business-as-usual compensation for deferral is not yet established nationally.

IEA recommends expanding viable DER business models (including VPP flexibility) precisely because routine compensation mechanisms are not yet in place; congestion management is currently handled largely through connection restrictions rather than DER payments.

No compensation available / market does not exist for any assets.

Ancillary service markets compensate reactive power/voltage support primarily from large generators. Distributed/BTM assets providing voltage services are not routinely compensated; BTM participation remains largely at pilot/technical discussion stage.

Review notes single-variety market structures and lagging price-signal transmission; distributed resource participation in voltage-type services is marginal relative to thermal-dominated provision.

Compensation available but not to all customers

Frequency regulation and reserve markets operate in multiple provinces, with independent energy storage stations included since 2022 (Shandong first). Compensation is largely limited to utility-scale and independent storage; aggregated BTM storage participation is emerging but not open to all customers.

Provinces have progressively expanded participants to include renewables, consumers and storage, but BTM household assets qualify rarely and typically only via aggregators meeting minimum size thresholds.

Compensation available but not to all customers

Peak-shaving is a compensated ancillary service in most provincial markets (with price caps, e.g. 450 CNY/MWh in one cited province), and demand charges/TOU differentials penalise peaks. Residential/BTM participation is via DR programmes and aggregators, not universally open.

Documents peak-shaving markets with published price caps and expanding participant scope; C&I demand response compensation is substantial in mature provinces (Guangdong, Jiangsu, Shanghai) per market analyses.

Compensation available but not to all customers

Spot price spikes now provide direct arbitrage signals for market participants, and emergency/price-responsive demand response is compensated in mature provinces. Household BTM systems cannot generally monetise this directly.

Describes substantial peak-shaving/frequency-regulation payments in provinces with mature spot and ancillary markets versus grid-mandated reliability programmes elsewhere — compensation exists but is regionally uneven.

No compensation available / market does not exist for any assets.

Black start is procured through planned, administratively designated arrangements with conventional plants; no open market accessible to BTM technology exists.

Review identifies black start among frontier ancillary varieties that remain at the stage of technical feasibility discussion and mechanism conception, lacking mature market design in China.

No compensation available / market does not exist for any assets.

Valley/off-peak TOU pricing implicitly rewards demand increase, but explicit compensated demand-increase service markets for BTM assets are not established.

Market reforms emphasise capturing flexibility value (energy, flexibility, capacity, environmental attributes) as a forward-looking goal rather than an existing national demand-increase product; no explicit BTM-accessible market identified in sources.

Compensation available but not to all customers

Market-based and ordered demand response programmes compensate load reduction in many provinces (driven by summer peaks), largely for C&I loads aggregated by DR platforms/VPPs; residential participation is limited.

Documents load aggregators/VPP operators providing peak-shaving and load-shifting DR across provinces with applicable capacity targets of ~5% of provincial maximum load per stage.

Compensation available but not to all customers

The Green Electricity Certificate (GEC) market now covers all renewables including distributed projects (with DPV market participation via aggregation expanding from 2025), and the national ETS covers the power sector. However, GEC prices have collapsed with oversupply, and household BTM systems generally access value only indirectly.

GECs are now China's sole renewable attribute certificate with expanded scope; 4.73 billion issued in 2024 with 446 million traded (see also REDEX). RMI notes green premiums have declined amid supply surge. Direct BTM monetisation remains uneven.

No compensation available / market does not exist for any assets.

Green power trading (bundled energy + certificates) is open to renewable generators and increasingly to aggregated distributed projects, but core capacity markets and capacity compensation are directed at thermal/utility-scale assets, not BTM.

Capacity compensation (100–165 yuan/kW/year) applies to coal units and expanded nationwide by 2024 — a market from which BTM assets are excluded.

No fee is payable

Self-consumed electricity is exempt from network charges, government surcharges and taxes; no fee is payable to any grid, network or system actor for self-consumption. Registration is free for household systems.

National policy direction explicitly encourages self-consumption as the primary model for distributed PV (reinforced by Document 136 market reforms); no evidence in sources of charges on self-consumed energy.

Some barriers to connecting and using behind-the-meter technology for self-consumption

Filing/registration is simple and online, but customers cannot connect freely where hosting capacity is exhausted: in 2024, congestion and connection restrictions were reported in 11 provinces (red zones), suspending new filings.

IEA documents the red/green/yellow hosting-capacity "alarm light" mechanism as a development prerequisite in restricted areas; connection caps in some jurisdictions also restrict C&I systems above 6 MW to full self-consumption.

Permitting is required but is simple and online

Registration (filing/备案) is online via utility platforms and has largely replaced discretionary permitting, but it remains a mandatory pre-installation step subject to grid hosting-capacity review, not a pure fit-and-inform regime.

NSR describes standardised working mechanisms for distributed renewable integration and streamlined grid-connection procedures; filings can nonetheless be postponed where distribution grid hosting capacity is exceeded.

Solar panel installs are permitted activities and building consents only apply to rooftop arrays above certain sizes

Rooftop solar is broadly a permitted activity in most zones, with the Whole County programme mandating installation percentages on public buildings. Restrictions apply mainly to specific protected/historic zones, aviation zones, and via size thresholds.

Documents the Whole County PV targets (50% of party/government buildings, 40% public, 30% C&I, 20% rural rooftops in participating counties), evidencing permissive planning posture at national level.

Interconnection application is required but is simple and online. Applications are processeed in less than 15 days.

Interconnection is free of charge for household DPV (no connection or system backup fees under national policy) and processed through standardised online channels, but processing is not fully automated and capacity-assessment queues in congested provinces delay connections beyond 15 days in practice.

NSR confirms streamlined procedures and "green channel" mechanisms, but hosting-capacity gating (Office 〔2023〕74 alarm-light system) and documented postponements mean the process is neither automated nor consistently fast for all applicants.

There is a database of network capacity / but it is not open to the public or does not show individual customers

The national grid hosting-capacity assessment mechanism publishes green/yellow/red zones at provincial/county level, giving location-specific capacity indications, but full feeder-level public datasets for customers are not uniformly open; some data is accessible only to or through developers/utilities.

Hosting capacity assessments rolled out nationwide in 2024 with the alarm-light publication mechanism as a development prerequisite; granularity and openness to individual customers vary by province.

Data available but is only for import or export or some customers

T&D tariffs and network charge structures are public and regulated, but customer-specific costs for increasing import/export capacity (upgrades, transformer reinforcement) are not published and are quoted case-by-case.

The T&D pricing regime (cost-plus reasonable profit) is transparent at the tariff level, but no public schedule of connection-point upgrade costs was identified in the sources.

Digital registration process in place which is at least regionalised

Yes — national online registration/filing platforms operated by State Grid and China Southern Grid allow digital registration of DPV assets, used nationwide across the Whole County programme.

Standardised, digitally administered registration of distributed PV is a core element of the documented standardisation of county-wide rooftop PV development.

System operator cannot dispatch with more than 20% of total electricity generation from behind the meter tech at any one time

China is building grid-forming storage capability and new-type power system pilots, but BTM generation represents a minority of dispatchable supply; wind and solar combined reached ~22% of generation in 2025 and system dispatch is not structured around 70% BTM sourcing.

Ember data: 42% of electricity from clean sources in 2025, wind and solar 22%. DPV is ~40% of solar capacity but system dispatch remains centrally managed around conventional and utility-scale resources; 70% BTM dispatch is far from current practice.

Some localised rules and some national/statewide rules

National GB/GB-T standards and NDRC/NEA market rules govern grid connection, dispatch interfaces and market participation, but substantive implementation varies across provincial markets and pilots.

National technical standards for distributed PV connection and market rules exist; ancillary-services research repeatedly flags large inter-provincial rule differences, with "one game of chess" national unification as a stated goal rather than completed fact.

Some localised rules and some national/statewide rules

National metering and data-exchange standards (smart meter specifications, dispatch data protocols) are set at national level with near-universal meter deployment, but exchange with third parties (VPP platforms, retailers) follows provincial market rules.

IEA recommends capacity building and best-practice exchange, indicating interoperability/data governance between BTM assets, system operators and aggregators is maturing rather than settled; smart meter data infrastructure itself is national-standardised.

Best practices and standards in place which are continually (at least annually) reviewed and align to international best practice and standards

National mandatory and recommended standards (GB/NB/T series) govern PV system design, installation and grid connection, aligned substantially with IEC international norms, with periodic revision cycles.

China participates in IEA-PVPS and applies national technical standards for distributed PV; standards undergo scheduled revisions, and grid-connection acceptance enforces electrical standards.

Best practices and standards in place which are continually (at least annually) reviewed and align to international best practice and standards

National electrical safety codes, fire safety requirements and grid-connection acceptance testing apply nationwide, with enforcement through utility inspection before energisation and occupational safety regulation of installers.

Grid-connection procedures include safety verification; standards are nationally uniform rather than locally fragmented, though enforcement intensity at village level has been flagged in rural deployment literature.

Tariffs on imported behind-the-meter technology <10%

Imports of BTM technology are marginal given China's domestic manufacturing dominance; applied duty rates on solar components are low (modules at or near zero MFN), placing effective tariff levels well below 10%.

Documents China's overwhelming domestic manufacturing dominance in solar PV, making imports a residual flow; no evidence in sources of border tariffs ≥10% on solar modules or residential storage equipment. I'm not aware of any source documenting a specific BTM-technology-specific tariff schedule, hence the residual score.

Tax incentives or subsidies are available for behind-the-meter technology but are less than those provided to utility scale technology or other energy technology

Direct national subsidies for household PV ended with the FiT phase-out. Remaining supports (VAT relief on PV, GEC income, local subsidies in some provinces, appliance trade-in programme) are modest relative to the auction-priced, capacity-compensated and green-premium supports available to utility-scale projects.

Confirms subsidy phase-outs; Document 136 removed guaranteed pricing for new projects across the board, while capacity compensation (100–165 yuan/kW/year) accrues to thermal/utility assets, not household BTM (per PMC power sector reform study).

Some in house Equipment supplier / Industry body qualifications offered for behind-the-meter technology installation and maintenance
